A drain that ended on a full group, an oversized frame or a `Barrier` could reach a blocking `receive` with END behind e, and stay there while the writer was quiet. v2.92 adds a rule: before any blocking `receive`, if the last END written is below e, the task writes END(e) first. So once the queue is empty, `d` = e. Live capture depends on that (below). It costs at most one extra END per return to idle, off the ack path. **L94:** with `end_interval_ms = 0` this rule holds as written. With `end_interval_ms > 0` (default 10 ms), END is written before a blocking wait only once it is due (`end_groups` groups past END, or `end_interval_ms` after the oldest unnamed acked group); until then the wait is `receive_until` with that due time, so `d` reaches `e` within `end_interval_ms` of the queue going quiet, plus at most one group (§3.3).
- **END.** After the ack: `write_at(end_file, 0, END(d))` on the `Durable` handle, with no `sync`. END stays 96 bytes, unaligned and buffered, because its readers (`disk_read_end`, `store.hirsel:4644`) parse every byte to EOF, and zero padding there would fail them. It reaches io-wq on ext4 (K2) and is off the ack path, as before.
- **Barrier `Written` (W2).** It is answered when the group's write completes. That now also means durable, which W2 allows.

**The segment fence (v2.95; writers and openers revised, reader protocol rewritten by v2.98).** v2.92 argued that exit drains the ring before `LOCK` is released. On Linux v7.0 that is false for direct I/O, so the handoff needs its own fence.
- **The kernel facts (v7.0, 028ef9c).**
  - `do_exit` runs `io_uring_files_cancel()` (`kernel/exit.c:916`) before `exit_files` (`:971`). That is `__io_uring_cancel(false)` (`include/linux/io_uring.h:17-20`).
  - With `cancel_all` false, the wait loop breaks as soon as `inflight_tracked` is 0 (`io_uring/cancel.c:566-570`, `:598`). Only requests on an io_uring file are tracked (`io_uring/io_uring.c:1579-1585`, `io_req_track_inflight` at `:334-340`).
  - A direct `WRITE` or `WRITEV` on a regular file returns -EIOCBQUEUED and completes later from the block layer (`io_rw_done`, `io_uring/rw.c:618-624`). Nothing in exit waits for it, so its bytes can reach the device after `LOCK`'s file closes.
  - `flock` belongs to an open file description (OFD), so `LOCK`'s release fences nothing on a segment's OFD.
- **What does outlive every request.** The file a request names.
  - `io_file_get_normal` takes a reference with `fget` (`io_uring/io_uring.c:1575-1577`), and `io_put_file` drops it when the request is freed, after its completion (`:1111`, `io_uring/io_uring.h:383-386`).
  - A direct write with O_DSYNC runs `generic_write_sync` before `ki_complete` (`fs/iomap/direct-io.c:150-151`, `:166`). So when a request completes **successfully**, its bytes are durable.
  - **A failed completion is not durable (2249 M4).** A write can complete with an error after its data bios are done, when the flush or the journal commit failed. Its bytes are then on the device, readable and possibly only in the volatile cache.
  - A task that has exited still frees its requests. When `task_work_add` fails on an exiting task, completion work goes to the ring's `fallback_work` (`io_uring/tw.c:261-264`, `:88-106`), a kernel workqueue that runs it (`:18-30`).
  - The OFD's `flock` is removed only in `__fput`, when the last reference drops (`fs/file_table.c:461`, `locks_remove_file`; `fs/locks.c:2767-2789`).
  - So **an exclusive `flock` on the OFD a segment is written through is held until every write issued through it has completed, even after its process has died.** Completed means durable only for a write that succeeded. That is why every read under a free fence follows a sync (below).
- **What a free fence means (v2.98).** `try_lock_shared` on a segment succeeds exactly when no handle holds the segment exclusive. Then:
  - (i) every write ever issued to the segment has completed, successfully or not;
  - (ii) if the segment's HEADER is good, no handle will ever write it again.
  - (ii) holds because the segment's only writers are its creator and its journal task, which share one handle. That handle holds the fence from before the creation block until it closes. An open never appends to a segment it did not create (§3.4 step 8).
  - So **a good-header segment whose fence is free holds its final bytes.** The one segment that is rewritten after its fence is free is a torn-header one, which step 8 re-creates. No reader ever fences one (below).
- **The writers.**
  - The creator (genesis, open step 8, cut step 1) opens the segment `Direct` and takes `try_lock` on that handle before it writes the creation block. It hands that same handle to the journal task. No other handle writes the segment.
  - **The creator's poll.** While `try_lock` answers false, the creator sleeps 1 ms on the open's clock and tries again, with no deadline.
    - Readers take no fence on a segment without a good HEADER (below), and openers fence only under the same `LOCK`. So the only holder a creator can meet is a dead creator's in-flight creation block on the same inode.
    - That happens at genesis over a dead genesis's `j-1`. It also happens at step 8 over a torn-header segment, but there step 5's take has already waited the block out, so the poll answers at once. A cut's new segment has never existed, so no one holds its fence.
    - The wait is therefore one device write, which a hung device stretches no further than it stretches a `sync`.
    - v2.95's stall by a stopped reader, and the logged decision that accepted it, are deleted: no reader can hold a fence that a creator needs (2249 M1).
  - **The journal task closes its segment handle once its last write completes.** It does so at rotation (§3.3), at `close`, at drop (§1.10), and when it ends with `Failed(e)` (§3.8). The close releases the fence. A poisoned Db keeps `LOCK` but holds no segment handle (BL6).
  - Both backends, the sim fs and the crash bridge follow the rule. On a helper host a `pwrite` keeps its thread, and with it the file, alive until it returns. A synchronous direct write waits in TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE until its bios finish (`fs/iomap/direct-io.c:860-868`), so even SIGKILL cannot end the thread first. So the fence holds there too, and a helper-host opener waits out a ring-host owner the same way.
- **The opener (amends §3.4 step 5).** Under `LOCK`, `open` takes `try_lock_shared` on each segment's read handle before it syncs and reads that segment. Shared is enough, because only an exclusive holder (a writing handle) can have writes in flight. It also lets the opener pass a reader's shared fence without waiting.
  - This covers every segment step 5 opens. That includes a last segment with a bad header, which step 5 treats as absent and step 8 re-creates with `Write`. Without the take, a dead owner's creation block landing after the re-creation would overwrite the new owner's first frames.
  - **The wait.** While `try_lock_shared` answers false, the opener sleeps 1 ms on the open's clock and tries again, with **no deadline**. `lock_wait_ms` governs `LOCK` only, so a fence never makes `open` return `Held`.
  - **Who can hold the fence exclusive under `LOCK`.** Only a dead owner's request still at the device. No live process holds a segment's fence without `LOCK`:
    - `close` joins the journal task before it drops `LOCK`;
    - a drop waits for each task before the `LOCK` file closes (§1.10);
    - a failed journal task closes its handle (§3.8).
    So the wait ends when the device completes that write. A device that never completes it would hang the open's `sync` the same way.
  - **Decision (logged; reversible, one rule).** The fence wait takes no deadline. Right after a kill, a deadline would turn a draining write into `Held`.
  - The opener releases the fence (`unlock`, then close) when it has read the segment. A dead owner can issue nothing more, and step 8 writes only new segments.
  - **Why the sync runs after the fence (2249 M4).** A free fence means every write has completed, not that every write is durable. A write that completed with an error left bytes that are readable and that a power cut can take back.
    - The sync after the fence either makes those bytes durable or fails, and a failure ends the open with `Io(e)`. A flush covers every command completed before it. On ext4, an fsync of a clean inode still sends one: `jbd2_trans_will_send_data_barrier` returns 0 for a committed transaction, so `blkdev_issue_flush` runs (`fs/ext4/fsync.c:123-125`, `:177-179`).
    - Without the sync, the opener could name a failed write's bytes in `prev_end`, and a power cut would then make the store `Corrupt(Truncated)`.
    - So the sync is required on every provider (BL13). v2.95's two reasons for it (segments written before v2.92, and the O_DSYNC-only fallback) are withdrawn, because readers accept only the current format.
  - **Residual (page cache; stated, not new).** This applies only on a page-cache write path: the O_DSYNC-only fallback, or ext4's buffered fallback of a direct write.
    - There a failed write can leave pages readable in the page cache that never reached the device.
    - A later fsync on another descriptor may not report the error once the writer has seen it (`errseq`). That is §3.8's known limit, which now also covers a new process in the same boot.
    - It reaches only frames past the last successful write, and those were never acked. Store does not defend past it, and a reboot clears it.
- **Op classes at a dead owner's exit, and what covers each.**

| Op class (ring host) | Where it runs | What covers it before the next owner reads |
|---|---|---|
| direct `WRITE`/`WRITEV` on a segment (`write_at`, `zero_at`, the creation block) | inline issue, completion from the block layer | **the segment fence** (above), then the reader's or opener's sync for a write that failed |
| buffered `WRITE` on `Durable`/`Write` handles (END, packs, MANIFEST.tmp, export scratch, other programs' files such as `session_u`'s partition log) | io-wq: ext4 lacks `FOP_BUFFER_WASYNC` in v7.0 (`fs/ext4/file.c:975-977`), so io_uring punts the write at issue (`io_uring/rw.c:1150-1154`); otherwise inline in the issuing thread | exit: `io_uring_clean_tctx` → `io_wq_put_and_exit` waits for every io-wq worker inside `io_uring_files_cancel` (`io_uring/tctx.c:207-224`, `io_uring/io-wq.c:1338-1371`, `:1394-1399`), so before `exit_files`. An inline op finished before its thread could exit |
| `FSYNC` (SYNC, SYNC_DIR), `RENAMEAT`, `UNLINKAT`, `MKDIRAT`, `STATX`, creating `OPENAT2` | io-wq always (the list above) | exit, as the row above |
| non-creating `OPENAT2`, `CLOSE`, `TRY_LOCK`, `TRY_LOCK_SHARED`, `UNLOCK` | inline | the issuing thread's own exit order |
| buffered `READ` | inline or task work | changes nothing on disk |
| helper syscalls (`off_slot`, helper hosts) | a Hirsel thread in the syscall | the thread holds the file table until the syscall returns. An uninterruptible direct `pwrite` finishes first |

  So among a dead owner's mutations, only direct writes can still be in flight once `LOCK` is free, and only segments are written directly. The END file is buffered `Durable`, so exit covers it.
  - The ring is set up without SQPOLL and registers no fixed files (`crates/hirsel-core-net/src/reactor/uring/ring.rs:242-251`, and its only registrations, `:34-37`, are the probe, buffers and io-wq workers). Both are build constraints for fenced handles (BL18): a fixed-file request holds the file through its resource node instead (`io_uring/rsrc.c:496-503`), which this section does not argue.
- **What the fence costs.** No write pays anything for it. The inline lock calls are:
  - one `try_lock` per segment creation;
  - one `try_lock_shared` per segment an open reads;
  - one `try_lock_shared` per reader capture, on the terminal segment, plus a `LOCK` probe only when that is refused.
  The per-write cost stays v2.92's: about 19 µs for an in-window group write and 89 µs extending (K4). For a buffered program write such as `session_u`'s partition log, the ring route stays at a1-regress-2209's 11.0 µs per op, against 16.2–18.5 µs for the helper hop and 4.2–4.5 µs inline.

**Reader captures (v2.98; replaces v2.95's "Readers without `LOCK`"; closes 2249 B1, M1, M2, M3).** This covers every read that takes no `LOCK`: a log@1 follower's first capture, `catch_up`, each poll of `at_least`, `fresh`, and `open_read_only` in `Live`. Readers take only shared locks and never write, so readers never exclude each other. Each capture runs these steps:
1. **Walk.** Read MANIFEST whole. Then, for n = `first_live`, `first_live` + 1, …, open `j-<n>` until NotFound, reading its END file first and then its HEADER.
   - **The order matters.** The creator writes the HEADER block, then END(72) (the barrier table). So an END that reads good implies that the HEADER read after it is the creator's. A reader that read the HEADER first could see a bad HEADER, then a good END, mid-creation, and report a false `Corrupt(Header)` (BL7).
   - When the segment is the last one opened (`j-<n+1>` is NotFound), a short or bad HEADER with a missing or bad END means the segment is absent, and the walk ends before it, as in §3.4 step 5. A bad HEADER with a good END is `Corrupt(Header)`, as is a bad HEADER on any segment that has a successor.
   - The last segment present is the **terminal** segment. Each earlier segment is bounded by its successor's `prev_end`.
   - **No fence is taken during the walk, and none is ever taken on a segment without a good HEADER (2249 M1).**
2. **Bound.** Take `try_lock_shared` on the terminal segment's read handle.
   - **Granted: the torn-tail bound.** The segment's bytes are final (what a free fence means, above).
   - **Refused:** probe `LOCK` with `try_lock_shared` on a `Read` handle, then `unlock` at once. A missing `LOCK` file counts as free.
     - **`LOCK` held: the END bound.** A live journal task is writing the segment.
     - **`LOCK` free:** an exclusive holder without `LOCK` is a dead owner's request still at the device. The reader sleeps 1 ms and repeats step 2, within the call's deadline. `open_read_only` has no deadline and waits like the opener. At the deadline the call returns its deadline result (`Behind`, or `Remote(Retriable(Deadline))` mapped as today) and publishes nothing new.
   - **`LOCK` matters only when the fence is refused.** Once no handle writes the terminal segment, an open owner changes nothing. So a reader reads to the torn tail beside a poisoned owner whose journal task has ended (2249 M3). It does the same beside an opener in steps 2–7 that has not yet created its segment, which removes B1's first trigger (below).
3. **Gate.** The **capture key** is the MANIFEST bytes' digest, the segment numbers walked, the terminal END file's bytes (or its absence), and the bound.
   - If the key equals the key of this follower's last capture attempt, the capture repeats that attempt's outcome, whether it was published or kept by the monotone rule. It reads no segment and issues no `sync_dir` and no sync. It still revalidates the packs against the MANIFEST, as v2.71 does.
   - An attempt that ended in an error records no key.
   - The worker keeps the key. Why the key is enough is under "The capture key", below.
4. **Read** (a changed key).
   - First `sync_dir` (O1, §12.5). Then re-read MANIFEST: if its bytes differ from those the key digested, the capture restarts at step 1. So the MANIFEST a capture publishes was read after a `sync_dir` that covers its name.
   - **Torn-tail bound.** The reader keeps the fence and syncs the terminal segment. The sync is required, because a free fence means completed, not durable (M4, BL13). It then reads past `d` to the first bad frame as §3.4 step 5 does, and unlocks.
   - **END bound.** The reader holds no fence and issues no segment sync. It applies only frames of the terminal segment that end at or below that segment's END `d` (the END bound, below).
   - **Middle segments** are read to their successor's `prev_end`, with no sync on either bound. Their bytes below `prev_end` were durable before the successor's HEADER named it (§3.5 step 0, §3.4 step 5), and that holds even across a successor HEADER that is visible before it is durable.
5. **Publish.** The worker passes the candidate through the monotone rule (below), and the caller's swap publishes it (§12.5 "One publication point").

- **What each bound publishes.**
  - The torn-tail bound publishes exactly what a §3.4 recovery would recover at that moment, because the bytes are final and synced.
  - The END bound publishes only frames whose writes completed successfully, because `d` follows the ack.
  - Neither publishes a frame that a power cut can take back, apart from the page-cache residual above, which affects the torn-tail bound only.
- **An owner that opens during a capture.** The owner takes `LOCK` and rotates.
  - Until its step 8 segment's END reads good, the reader's terminal is the old segment. That segment's fence is free, or held shared by step 5, so the reader reads its final bytes to the torn tail.
  - After that, the new segment is the terminal one, its creator holds the fence, and the bound is END. The old segment is then bounded by the new HEADER's `prev_end`, which is the stop step 5 found in the same final bytes.
  - Either way the candidate is at or ahead of anything a previous capture published.
- **A cut during a capture.** The creator holds the new segment's fence before it writes. The old segment's journal task holds the old one's until its last write completes, after `Rotate`, and the cut began only after X1.
  - Suppose a reader walked before the new segment existed and finds the old fence free. It then reads final bytes whose torn-tail stop is the e the writer counted, and that e is the new `prev_end`.
- **What a reader can cost an owner.**
  - Readers fence only good-header segments, and only shared. So a reader never delays a creator, and an opener's shared take passes it.
  - **Decision (logged; reversible).** An opener with `lock_wait_ms` = 0 makes one `LOCK` attempt. That attempt can meet a reader's shared `LOCK` probe, which the reader holds across two inline calls and makes only when the terminal fence was refused. The opener then returns `Held`, an explicit refusal.
    - Under §12.5's exclusion no opener runs beside a reader. Beside one, `lock_wait_ms` > 0 polls past it.
    - To reverse it, drop the probe and accept that a `fresh` beside a live writer waits.
  - A poll whose key has not changed costs file reads of MANIFEST and of each segment's END and HEADER, one inline `try_lock_shared`, and at most one `LOCK` probe. It sends no flush to the writer's device (2249 M2).

**The monotone rule (v2.98; closes 2249 B1).** A follower's published state never moves backwards on any branch. The worker compares each candidate C with the published capture P that the request names:
- **C is behind P** when, for some branch id b < `P.next_branch`, any of these holds:
  - P holds b at version v and C holds b below v;
  - P holds b and C has not seen it (`C.next_branch` ≤ b);
  - `C.next_branch` < `P.next_branch`.
  A branch that P holds and C does not, with `C.next_branch` > b, was deleted or adopted in C's history. That counts as forward, not behind.
- **C is behind and END-bounded** (an old `d`, an unreadable terminal END giving `d` = 72, or an END read racing its rewrite). C is not published, and the worker answers `Captured(None)`:
  - P stays published;
  - `catch_up` returns P's position;
  - `fresh` returns P's snapshot at once, which matters because the projector calls it with no deadline;
  - `at_least` keeps polling.
- **C is behind and torn-tail-bounded, or C is an objects@1 candidate.** The answer is `Diverged(b)`, where b is the lowest branch id by which C is behind, and P stays published.
  - A torn-tail bound reads final, synced bytes that a §3.4 recovery would also read. objects@1 follows a linearizable head chain (§12.2).
  - So a behind candidate of either kind means the store lost what the follower showed: media damage (D6, §3.4) or the page-cache residual.
- **Otherwise C goes to the caller's swap.**
- **One place.** This replaces the main-only guards in `catch_up` and `fresh` (`store-followers.hirsel:291-293`, `:304`). The comparison moves into the worker, covers every branch, and is the only place a candidate is refused for order. `at_least` and `fresh` get it the same way.
- **B1's two triggers.**
  - **Torn tail, then END over the same segment, can no longer happen.** A terminal segment read to the torn tail had a free fence, so it will never be written again, and the next owner's segment carries the same stop as its `prev_end`. That trigger is gone by construction of the bound (step 2), not by this rule.
  - **An unreadable or racing terminal END** beside a live writer still yields `d` = 72 or an old `d`. This rule keeps P, and it is the only mechanism for that trigger.
  - Both triggers are B1's NO-GO traces. BL9 checks both.

**The capture key (v2.98; replaces the v2.82 journal witness; 2249 M2).** v2.82's `log_journal_witness` (`store-manifest.hirsel:961`) synced and hashed every live segment on each capture, so that equal witnesses implied equal recovery results. Each `at_least` poll therefore sent 1 + segments flushes to the writer's device. Two facts make the key enough:
- bytes below an END's `d` are acked, and are only ever rewritten with the same bytes (the tail image);
- a good-header segment with a free fence is final.

So an equal key implies an equal candidate. The exception is media damage between captures, which a reused capture does not re-detect, as before. `log_journal_witness`, `witness_terminal`, `witness_range`, `witness_word`, the `journal` field of `LogFollowWitness` and v2.95's bound bit are deleted. So are the witness cases in `store_journal_laws_4.hirsel` (`window_law_witness` and its checks, ~600-670): the machinery they checked is gone. The worker keeps the key of its last attempt, published or kept, so a terminal END that stays unreadable costs one recapture, not one per 10 ms poll.

**Why rewriting the tail block is safe.** Each group rewrites up to 4,095 bytes of frames that are already acked: the [⌊e⌋ₐ, e) prefix of R.
- The bytes written there equal the bytes on disk (the tail image is exact, above). So under the sector-atomicity assumption every crash cut leaves each sector old or new, and both are the same acked bytes.
- **The sector-atomicity assumption.** A sector a crash interrupts reads back as its old or its new content.
- That is the assumption the store held before v2.92. ext4 writeback of a buffered append writes the whole 4 KiB block too, acked prefix included. So v2.92 adds no exposure, and a device that tears inside a sector already breaks the old path.
- A frame-aligned layout that never rewrites acked bytes would pad each group with a skippable frame. That is NOT TAKEN (prior art, below): unknown non-required kinds are bounded by `UNKNOWN_ROOM` (1 MiB per segment, `store.hirsel:4661`), so it would need a new kind and a reader change.

**A torn direct write, and recovery** (§3.4 step 5 reads every case unchanged).
- **Crash with a group write in flight or partly persisted.**
  - R's sectors may persist in any subset.
  - Sectors below e hold the same bytes either way.
  - Sectors in [e, ⌈e + g⌉ₐ) hold new frame bytes, the window's durable zeros, or (past the old file end) nothing visible.
  - Recovery reads from `d` ≤ e and stops at the first bad frame, so it recovers a run of whole frames from e, each of whose bytes in the image are the bytes written, and nothing after the first gap. That is §3.3a's "a group cut inside the window", unchanged. None of the group was acked, because its ack waits for completion.
- **Crash with the write submitted but its CQE not yet received.** The same image set, since completion only tells the writer the I/O happened. The writer is dead, so it sent no ack.
  - **v2.95: exit does not wait for it.** v2.92 said the ring's teardown waits for every request in flight before the files close. On v7.0 that holds only for tracked requests, and a direct write is not one (the segment fence, above). `LOCK` can pass while the write is still at the device.
  - **The segment fence orders it.** The opener takes each segment's fence before it syncs and reads. The fence is free only once the dead writer's write has completed. The opener's sync then makes durable whatever a failed completion left readable, or it fails (v2.98, 2249 M4). Only then does the opener read and set `prev_end`.
  - Without the fence, the opener could read the write's bytes from the device's volatile cache and name them by `prev_end`. Its sync's flush covers only commands completed before the flush, so a power cut would leave the old segment shorter than `prev_end`, which is `Corrupt`. A torn-header segment re-created by step 8 could also take the dead creation block over its new frames.
- **The padded tail.** Its zeros lie past e. If they persist, recovery reads a kind-0 head at e+: torn, the stop. If they don't, the bytes there are the window's earlier zeros or past EOF. Either way the stop is at or before e + g.
- **Pieces of a large frame.** A crash after some pieces leaves the frame's head and part of its payload, so its check fails or it is short. That is torn past `d`, never `Corrupt`, because `d` ≤ e.
- **END older than its data.** END is written after the ack, so `d` ≤ the last acked e at every cut. A crash after a group and before the next END leaves `d` behind e. Recovery reads past `d` to the torn tail, as before v2.92. An END can never be newer than its data: `d` names an e whose writes completed successfully, and a successful `Durable` or `Direct` completion is durable (a failed one is EIO and poisons before any END names it).
- **Window step cut short.** `zero_at` persists any subset of its sectors over a region past w that is absent or zero. It lies past every frame (§3.6 row "window step", unchanged).

**EIO and short writes.**
- **Reads.** A ring `READ` returns n > 0 bytes, 0 at EOF, or an error.
  - A short read is not an error: the host returns the bytes it got, as `read`/`read_at` already may (`docs/spec/core.md`).
  - An unreadable page gives `Other(5)` (EIO) for the read that reaches it. The host never fills zeros, and never returns bytes from a page the kernel did not read.
  - A Tiered page read or a journal scan that hits it fails like any failed host read. Other pages are unaffected, and a later read of the same page is a new read.
  - This differs from TigerBeetle, which zero-fills an unreadable sector and treats it as a checksum failure (prior art). In Store a zero run is a kind-0 head, the torn tail: a zero-filled page below `d` would read as `Corrupt`, and one past `d` would silently end recovery early.
- **Writes.** A ring `WRITE`, `WRITEV` or helper `pwrite` that completes with n:
  - n = the requested length: done.
  - 0 < n < length, and (on a `Direct` handle) at + n a multiple of A: the host submits the rest at at + n. Each part is durable at its completion, so the call is durable when the last part completes. This is TigerBeetle's rule (prior art).
  - 0 < n < length with at + n not a multiple of A on a `Direct` handle: `Other(5)` (EIO). The rest could not be issued aligned.
  - n = 0: `Other(5)` (EIO), as `write_all_from` does today.
  - −EAGAIN or −EINTR: resubmit the same SQE (TigerBeetle `linux.zig:611-620`).
  - Any other negative result, ENOSPC included: that error.
  - A failed write is a failed write of the segment, so it poisons the store with no retry (§3.8). With O_DSYNC, a write error is also the sync failure: there is no later sync to report it.

**Every `host.sync` and `sync_dir` in Store, after v2.92.**

| Site | Before | v2.92 |
|---|---|---|
| group commit (journal task) | `write_at` + `sync` | one `Direct` `write_at`; no sync |
| window step | Z-chunk writes + `sync` | one `zero_at`; no sync |
| END write | `write_at` + `sync` | `Durable` `write_at`; no sync |
| segment creation (open step 8, cut step 1, genesis) | HEADER + `sync`, END + `sync`, `sync_dir` | HEADER block `Direct`, END `Durable`, `sync_dir` (ring `FSYNC`) |
| pack and `MANIFEST.tmp` (`disk_write_synced`, `disk_publish_manifest`) | `write` + `sync`, rename, `sync_dir` | unchanged; ring `FSYNC` |
| open step 5 and `Locked` readers (`journal_input(.., true)`) | `sync` each segment | unchanged, after the fence; ring `FSYNC`. Required, because a free fence means completed, not durable (BL13) |
| reader captures (follower, `Live` `open_read_only`) | v2.83, v2.84: `sync` each segment, then the terminal one again before publishing | **v2.98:** the terminal segment once, after its fence, and only on the torn-tail bound. There is none on the END bound and none for middle segments, and an unchanged capture key costs nothing at all (BL10) |
| export scratch, `EXPORT`, prepare | `write` + `sync`, `sync_dir` | unchanged; ring `FSYNC` |
| other programs' `host.sync` | helper pool | ring `FSYNC`, or `off_slot` on a helper host |

The briefed "FSYNC only for `sync_dir`" holds for the journal path. It does not hold for the store as a whole: pack, MANIFEST, export and open syncs keep FSYNC, because each follows many writes and is off the commit path.

**The END bound (amends §3.2 "live capture" and v2.83/v2.84; scoped by v2.98 to a terminal segment whose fence a live writer holds).** A reader without `LOCK` uses the END bound only when the terminal segment's fence is refused and `LOCK` is held (Reader captures, step 2). It then applies only frames of the terminal segment that end at or below that segment's END `d`, by the rules that follow.
- Middle segments stay bounded by the successor's `prev_end`.
- The reader reads END, then reads the segment to `d`. A segment shorter than `d` gets v2.83's one size refresh on the same handle, then is `Truncated`. A missing or bad END means `d` = 72.
- No sync: neither v2.83's second one nor the first, on any segment (2249 M2).
- **A damaged END under the END bound.** If the terminal END is unreadable, the candidate stops at `d` = 72 and, if that is behind what was published, the monotone rule keeps the published capture until the writer's next END rewrites the file whole. This costs freshness, not data, and never a false `Diverged`. A `Locked` open still reads past `d` to the torn tail (§3.4, "What a damaged END file costs"), so for recovery a damaged END still costs only detection.
- **Laws to revisit (build lane, BL18).** These cases read a live writer's terminal segment and may expect frames past END: `follower_crash_laws.hirsel` (`disk_crash_live_read_main`, `disk_crash_live_read_write`), and the Live cases in `store_crash_laws.hirsel`, `tiered_open_laws.hirsel` and `bucket_laws.hirsel`. Each such expectation becomes "applied at most to `d`" while the writer's journal task holds the fence, and none is weakened past that.
- **Scope.** The objects@1 journal (`store-object-journal.hirsel`, `ObjectFresh`) keeps its current write and sync discipline in v2.92. Moving it is a separate step.
- **Why.** v2.83's argument was that the reader's own sync makes durable every byte it read, because those bytes were dirty pages in the page cache.
  - A direct write puts its bytes on the device before they are durable. A concurrent buffered read can fetch them from the device's volatile cache while the write is still in flight.
  - The reader's later flush covers only commands completed before it was submitted. So the reader could publish a frame that a power cut takes back.
  - `d` names only bytes whose writes completed successfully, and on these handles that means durable. So the bound needs no claim about device or page-cache order, and no sync.
- It applies on both backends, so like readers read alike.
- **Cost and lag.** The lag exists only while a live journal task holds the terminal segment's fence.
  - **Beside a live writer** a follower trails it by the frames since the last END: at most 64 groups under load, and nothing once the writer's queue is empty, because END is written before every blocking `receive` (above). **L94:** with `end_interval_ms > 0` (default 10 ms), a live END-bounded follower trails by at most `end_groups` groups and, once the writer is quiet, by at most `end_interval_ms` plus one group, until END is due, `Rotate`, or close (§3.3).
  - **Beside a poisoned owner** there is no lag. Its journal task closed its handle when it failed, so the next capture reads to the torn tail (Reader captures, step 2).
  - **`at_least`** re-captures on each 10 ms poll (§12.5), and an unchanged key costs no flush.
  - **`fresh`** beside a live writer returns its END-bounded capture at once, or the published one under the monotone rule. Under exclusion it waits out a dead owner's last write by the fence.
- **Page-cache coherence for completed writes.** A direct write invalidates the range before (`fs/iomap/direct-io.c:765`) and after (`:139`) the I/O, so a buffered read that starts after completion sees the new bytes.
  - The invalidation after the I/O can fail. The kernel then only warns (`mm/filemap.c:4229-4237`) and can leave a stale tail-block folio below `d`. Rows 19 and 26 depend on it (BL16).

**Every reader of a segment's file size.**
- **Recovery scan** (§3.4 step 5, `journal_input`, `store.hirsel:5788-5800`): the size bounds reads and checks "shorter than `d`". Padding lengthens files only past e, so this is unchanged.
- **Live/follower refresh** (`journal_refresh_size`, `store-journal-recover.hirsel`): it refreshes the bound before `Truncated`. With END-bounded capture the boundary is `d` ≤ the durable e ≤ size, so a refresh matters only for a reader racing segment creation. Unchanged.
- **Follower witness**: deleted by v2.98 ("The capture key", above). The key reads no segment's size.
- **Export copy** (`store.hirsel:3871`, `replay_export`): it reads the scratch copy, which E1–E3 wrote through the captured terminal offset with `Write`, never the live padded file. The check `size > boundary` is unchanged.
- **`disk_read_paged_file`** (`store-manifest.hirsel:210`): it reads whole small files (MANIFEST, LOCK, END) by size, none of them `Direct`.
- **C-4 and `checkpoint_bytes`** count frames, not sizes (§11.11). Only the disk statement changes (Disk, above).
- **Tests that pin a size**: `store_journal_laws_4.hirsel:779` stats a segment. The build lane checks it against e, not the file size, where it means frames.

**Build laws (§3.3b) (v2.98).** The slot-ring build satisfies every law below and makes each check green. Each check names its harness, the real bug that turns it red, and its oracle. A **review** or **doc** law has no test. These are all durability or data-safety laws, so their reds block a push, except BL15's numbers, which ride (PLAN §5).
- **BL1. Both backends and a real disk.** The real-worker laws L3, L8 and L10 and the store law suites run once with `HIRSEL_NET_REACTOR=uring` and once with `=epoll`. The real-worker laws also run once on an ext4 directory under `/workspace` (O_DIRECT honoured), not only on `/dev/shm`. These are runs of existing laws, not new tests. The commit law (§3.3a) and L86's image contract are unchanged.
- **BL2. Tail-block images (case (a), L86).** For a group written over a tail block, build each crash image from every subset of R's 512-byte sectors, each old or new, and check acked ⊆ recovered ⊆ issued. Include the first group of a fresh segment (row 6a).
  - Bug: a tail image not refreshed after a group, which rewrites acked bytes with stale ones.
  - Oracle: the hand-derived image.
- **BL3. The host's alignment contract (case (b), the host file laws).** A `Direct` `write_at` with an unaligned offset, length or address returns `Other(22)` on tmpfs and in the sim fs.
  - Bug: a padding error that tmpfs would accept and ext4 would refuse in production.
  - Oracle: the contract.
- **BL4. The END bound (case (c), follower image case).** Use a hand-built directory whose terminal segment holds well-formed frames past its END's `d`.
  - With `LOCK` and the segment's fence held exclusive, a capture applies only the frames below `d`.
  - With both free, the same directory is read to the torn tail.
  - Bug: a reader that publishes in-flight direct bytes.
  - Oracle: the hand-built image.
- **BL5. The terminal fence decides the bound (2249 M3).** A capture tries the terminal fence first. Granted gives the torn tail whatever `LOCK`'s state. Refused with `LOCK` held gives the END bound. Refused with `LOCK` free means poll within the deadline.
  - Check, part 1: case (c) gets a third arm, with `LOCK` held and the fence free, which reads to the torn tail.
  - Check, part 2: a poison case in `follower_crash_laws.hirsel` on the sim fs. The writer acks 63 groups past its last END, and then the 64th group's own Direct write fails with ENOSPC, so the Db stays open and poisoned. (A window step cannot be the trigger: it runs only after an END write that covers every ack, so no window step fails while acks lie past END.) `at_least(position(t))` for the last acked t returns that branch's Snapshot.
  - Bug: an END-bounded capture under a held `LOCK`, which returns `Behind` until the process closes.
  - Oracle: the acked tickets (commit law).
- **BL6. A journal task that ends releases its fence, and a fenced-free segment is final (M3's premise).**
  - A journal task that ends by `Failed(e)`, `close` or drop closes its segment handle.
  - No handle writes a good-header segment after its fence has been free.
  - Check: BL5's poison case, which turns red if the failed task keeps its handle, because the capture is then END-bounded. The sim fs also fails the law on any write to a segment through a handle that does not hold its fence exclusive.
  - Bug: a handle kept or reopened past the task's end, which makes torn-tail reads unsound.
  - Oracle: the rule itself.
- **BL7. Header before fence, END before HEADER (2249 M1).** A reader reads each segment's END file and then its HEADER, and takes no fence on a segment without a good HEADER.
  - Check, part 1: a sim schedule case. The reader's walk runs between the creator's open of the new segment and its `try_lock` (2249 M1's trace), and the reader is then suspended right after step 2's fence take while the writer finishes the cut. The cut, and the commits queued behind it, complete while the reader stays suspended.
    - Bug: a reader that fences a fresh segment and stalls the creator.
    - Oracle: the spec's claim that no reader delays a creator.
  - Check, part 2: a reader interleaved at every schedule point of a segment creation never answers `Corrupt(Header)`.
    - Bug: HEADER read before END.
    - Oracle: no damage is injected.
- **BL8. The creator's poll has one cause (M1).** The poll stays with no deadline. The text and code that handle a stopped reader holding a fresh segment's fence are deleted.
  - Check: BL14, whose genesis arm is red without the creator's `try_lock`.
- **BL9. Monotone publication (2249 B1).** The worker applies the monotone rule and the caller-side guards at `store-followers.hirsel:291-293` and `:304` are deleted. Check: L57 (d) gains three arms.
  - **(i) The unreadable-END trigger.** A live writer holds `LOCK` and the fence. Publish a capture with main at m and side branch b at v+1, both below `d`. Then make the terminal END unreadable.
    - The next `catch_up`, `at_least` and `fresh` keep `applied(f, main)` and `applied(f, b)` unchanged, and none returns `Diverged`.
    - `fresh` with no deadline returns the published Snapshot at once.
  - **(ii) A behind torn-tail candidate.** With no writer, add a hand-built successor segment, with a free fence, whose `prev_end` lies below the published stop. The walk changes the capture key, the bound stays the torn tail, and the candidate is behind. (Damaging the terminal segment alone changes no key, so the gate would reuse the last attempt and the arm could not go red.) The answer is `Diverged(b)` with the lowest behind branch, and the published state stays.
  - **(iii) The restart trigger, on the crash bridge.** Kill the writer after acks past `d`. A follower captures to the torn tail. A new owner is then held in steps 2–7, and then after step 8. No branch's applied position decreases.
  - Bug: an END-bounded capture beside the held owner before the terminal fence is tried, or step 8 writing a `prev_end` below the acked tips. With a correct reader no candidate in this trace is behind, so (iii) cannot go red on the main-only guard; (i) and (ii) cover that guard.
  - Oracle: hand-derived branch tips.
- **BL10. The capture key, and no flush on the END bound (2249 M2).**
  - The key is as defined in "Reader captures".
  - An attempt with an equal key reads no segment and issues no `sync` and no `sync_dir`.
  - An END-bounded read issues no segment sync, and a torn-tail read syncs the terminal segment only.
  - The witness code and its cases are deleted.
  - Check, in the crash bridge, which already counts `segment_syncs` and the other syncs: an `at_least` that polls 10 times over a live store with an unchanged END issues 0 syncs. A changed END then costs 1 `sync_dir` and 0 segment syncs.
  - Bug: per-poll device flushes against the writer.
  - Oracle: the counts this law states.
- **BL11. The two-event write model, with per-handle locks (2249 H1).** The sim fs and the crash bridge implement the Terms rule "`Durable` and `Direct` in the sim fs and the crash bridge".
  - **Lock state is per handle on a file.** The file is the inode: it is kept across opens of the same name until it is removed, so a `Write` re-open of a torn-header segment keeps it.
  - Each file has a set of holders, each a handle with a shared or exclusive lock, under `flock`'s conflict rule.
  - A handle that a crash closes keeps its entry until its last pending write's complete event.
  - Today the bridge keys locks by name and exclusive only (`core/tools/store_crash_bridge.rs:43`, `:477-489`). The build replaces that map, adds `try_lock_shared`, and adds the readable and complete events.
  - Check: BL12–BL14 are red on their named bugs only with this model.
- **BL12. Case (d1): a late group landing (two events).** Kill the writer with a group's direct write issued and not complete, then open.
  - The bridge places the write's readable event at every schedule point of the new owner's open: before step 5's take, during its wait, and after. It places the complete event later.
  - A power cut falls after the new owner's first commit, at every point, including between readable and complete.
  - Oracle: the commit law, and the reopened store opens with no `Corrupt`.
  - Bug: an opener that reads before the fence. It names readable, non-durable bytes in `prev_end`, and the cut drops them, giving `Corrupt(Truncated)`.
- **BL13. Case (d2): a late landing that fails, and the sync after the fence (2249 M4).** This is (d1) with a failed complete event, whose readable sectors stay visible and not durable.
  - The opener and every torn-tail reader sync the segment after the fence, and before they read it, on every provider. A failed sync is `Io(e)`.
  - Oracle: as (d1).
  - Bug: an opener or reader that drops the sync because "a free fence means durable". It names the failed write's bytes, and the power cut drops them.
- **BL14. Case (d3): a creation block in flight (2249 H1, single event).**
  - **Arm 1 (cut).** Kill a cut's creator with its creation block issued on `j-k` and not yet readable, so `j-k` has a torn header. The new owner opens, and the block lands at every schedule point. The case is red only when both the opener's step-5 take and the creator's `try_lock` are missing.
  - **Arm 2 (genesis).** Kill a genesis with `j-1`'s creation block in flight. The case is red when the new genesis skips `try_lock`.
  - Oracle: the commit law over the new owner's acked frames.
  - Bug: a dead creation block landing over a re-created segment's first frames.
- **BL15. The gate, with a follower attached (2249 L1).** PLAN step 3's gate measures Store sync p50 and p99, and `off_slot` handoffs (0 during R8's commit and read phases, 1 per Store open), for R8 commits twice: alone, and with one log@1 follower polling `at_least`.
  - A follower's buffered read of the tail block caches it, and the next group write then takes -EAGAIN under NOWAIT and goes to io-wq (`mm/filemap.c:2904-2907`, `fs/iomap/direct-io.c:765-779`). That costs latency only.
  - The numbers ride, and durability reds block.
- **BL16. Page-cache invalidation can fail (review, 2249 L2).** Rows 19 and 26 rely on the invalidation after the I/O, which the kernel only warns about when it fails (`mm/filemap.c:4229-4237`).
  - A stale tail-block folio below `d` reads as `Corrupt` to an END-bounded reader, which then keeps its published state (a failed capture publishes nothing). The writer's own `recorded` read after `Barrier` would answer the same `Corrupt`.
  - The build surfaces the `Corrupt` and neither retries nor masks it. No test: the kernel offers no way to make the invalidation fail.
- **BL17. What `Direct` completion fences (doc, 2249 L3).** `docs/spec/core.md` §host files states it (this amend).
  - The completion of a `Direct` or `Durable` write on a handle means its bytes are durable when it succeeds.
  - A process's exit does not wait for its in-flight direct writes, so another process can run while they land.
  - A program that hands such a file to another process must order the handoff itself. Store does it with an exclusive `flock` on the writing handle, which the kernel holds until the last request on that handle completes.
- **BL18. Carried build constraints (v2.92, v2.95).**
  - No SQPOLL, and no fixed files, on fenced handles (row 31).
  - After a large frame written in pieces, copy [⌊e⌋ₐ, e) to the group buffer's head (row 24 (b)).
  - The MEM items of row 29: delete §11.11's idle release of the group buffer, and charge the creation block to the opener's limit.
  - The "laws to revisit" under the END bound.
  - `store_journal_laws_4.hirsel:779` checks e, not the file size.

**Expected effects [D].**
- **Group commit inside the window:** a pure direct overwrite with FUA, about 19 µs, against 96 µs for a buffered synced append (K4, measured microbench [M]). The store-level number is [D] until the gate measures it.
- **R8-open-i0:** workers-never-block-2157 took it from 130 to 180 ms (+38%) by routing every open-path file op through `off_slot`. Ring `OPENAT2`, `STATX`, `READ` and `CLOSE` complete without a helper thread handoff, and buffered reads that hit the page cache complete inline under COOP_TASKRUN. Path STAT, FSYNC, rename, remove and creating opens still hop to io-wq (the list above), so not all of the +50 ms comes back. The expectation is about 150–165 ms. This is [D], not derived from an op count, and the gate measures it. None of it is credited to O_DIRECT: open reads, and it does not write frames.
- **R6, R8-load:** small, from the same handoff removal, [D].

**Prior art.**
- **TigerBeetle** (`/tmp/ref-tigerbeetle` a2a3c70):
  - **O_DSYNC on every data-file write, so completion is durability: ADOPTED.** It is asserted at `src/stdx/io/linux.zig:1563-1564` and set at `:1456`, and `src/storage.zig` ~474 relies on it instead of fsync.
  - **Direct I/O where the file system supports it, probed at open: ADAPTED.** TigerBeetle probes at `linux.zig:1520-1532` and `:1784`, sets DIRECT for block devices at `:1498`, and skips tmpfs. With `direct_io_optional` it warns and falls back to O_DSYNC, otherwise it panics. Hirsel always falls back, because a store on any file system must open. It also enforces the alignment itself, which TigerBeetle gets from the kernel.
  - **Sector size 4,096: ADOPTED** (`src/stdx/io/common.zig:17`).
  - **Short writes continue, and EAGAIN/EINTR requeue: ADOPTED** (`storage.zig:409-448`, `linux.zig:611-620`). **A write EIO panics, and a zero-byte write panics: ADAPTED.** Hirsel poisons the store (§3.8), which reports the error and keeps snapshots readable.
  - **A read EIO is bisected by sector and the unreadable sector zero-filled: NOT TAKEN** (`storage.zig:251-310`). In Store, zeros are a frame-reader signal (the torn tail), so a fabricated zero is wrong data.
  - **WAL entries are sector-aligned slots: REPLACED.** Store packs frames and rewrites the tail block, because pad frames would need a new kind (the rewrite section above).
  - **fsync of the file and the directory at open: ADOPTED** as the existing creation barrier (`linux.zig:1652-1659` against §3.2).
  - **TigerBeetle's AOF writes without O_DIRECT** (`src/aof.zig:39`): no bearing.
- **Goose** (`/tmp/ref-goose` d5ae5bb) has no O_DIRECT, io_uring or fdatasync use: NOT TAKEN, nothing to take.
- **The segment fence (v2.95).**
  - TigerBeetle (a2a3c70) takes no `flock` in `src/`. Its data file has one process, which a crash ends together with its I/O as far as its replica protocol cares. **NOT TAKEN:** Store hands its directory to a new process, so it needs a fence.
  - Goose takes a blocking exclusive `flock` on a separate lock file (`src/process.cpp:160-172`), as Store's `LOCK` does. That fences processes, not I/O. **ADAPTED:** Store puts the same lock on the OFD that carries the I/O, so the kernel's request reference extends it.
- **The reader protocol (v2.98).**
  - Goose (d5ae5bb) has no follower and no second process that reads its files: **NOT TAKEN**, nothing to take.
  - TigerBeetle (a2a3c70) replicates over its replica protocol. No second process reads a replica's data file, so it needs neither a bound nor a gate: **NOT TAKEN**.
  - SQLite's WAL readers (known to me, not opened for this lane) read only up to the `mxFrame` that the wal-index publishes. That is the END bound, which v2.92 already ADAPTED. A SQLite reader never moves backwards, because a WAL reset waits for readers. Store's readers hold nothing a writer waits on, so Store gets the same property from the monotone rule at publication instead. **ADAPTED.**

**Self-attack (v2.92; v2.95 rewrites row 2, adds rows 23–29 for the items astra 2228 did not reach, and rows 30–32 against the fence; v2.98 rewrites rows 14, 23, 26, 28 and 30 to the current reader protocol and adds rows 33–41 for Fable 2249's findings).** Each row is an attack on this section and its answer. "Holds" means the answer is argued above. "Risk" marks an open point for the separate attack before any build.

Above e, each sector holds new frame bytes or the window's durable zeros. Recovery stops at the first frame whose image bytes differ from those written. That is v2.82's window row, and no part of the group was acked. | Holds, under the sector-atomicity assumption below |
